title: On Learned Ignorance
author: Nicholas of Cusa (Hopkins trans)
description: On Learned Ignorance (De docta ignorantia) by Nicholas of Cusa, in the English translation by Jasper Hopkins (Arthur J. Banning Press, 1981; 2nd ed. 1985), with notes. Completed in 1440, it is Cusanus's founding philosophical work. Book One treats the Absolute Maximum, God, as beyond all comparison and proportion, knowable only through a 'learned ignorance' that recognises the limits of reason; using mathematical symbols (the infinite line, triangle, circle and sphere), Cusanus shows how opposites coincide in the infinite. Book Two treats the universe as the 'contracted maximum', with famous anticipations of modern cosmology: the world has no fixed centre or circumference and the earth is not at rest. Book Three treats Jesus Christ as the maximum both absolute and contracted, uniting God and creation. A turning point between medieval mysticism and Renaissance philosophy, it influenced Bruno, Kepler and later speculative thought.
